title: Check yourself: what the compiler makes of a reference

questions.stem: Per this page, why does Comparator.comparing(Box::size).reversed() compile while Comparator.comparing(b -> b.size()).reversed() is rejected?

options.text: With no target type reaching it, the parameter b is inferred as Object
options.says: The page says the chained call gives the lambda no target type, so b is an Object without size(), while the reference carries its type.

options.text: With an int key inside it, b.size() is boxed, and boxed keys cannot reverse
options.says: Boxing is not the problem: the page offers comparingInt only to avoid boxing, and comparing(Box::size).reversed() works.

options.text: With a :: form inside it, the check waits for run time, so it passes now
options.says: The page says method references are checked by the compiler; the reference compiles because it names its class.

origin.section: Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

questions.stem: Per this page, how does a filter keep only the strings for which String::isBlank is false?

options.text: Put ! in front of it, as with any other boolean expression
options.says: The page shows filter(!String::isBlank) as a compile error.

options.text: Pass it to Predicate.not, which returns the opposite test
options.says: The page's idiomatic fix is filter(Predicate.not(String::isBlank)), available since Java 11.

options.text: Call .negate() on it directly, as :: already gives a Predicate
options.says: The page shows that calling a method such as andThen on a bare reference needs a cast first, since it has no type of its own.
